title: Chapter 24: The Malevolent 2
content:
Chapter 24

Jiang Cheng added coldly, "Lend me your dog."

Snapping out of his stupor, Jin Ling hesitated. But when Jiang Cheng's razor-sharp glare pinned him in place, the boy caved and blew a short whistle. The black-maned spiritual hound closed the distance in three bounds. Wei Wuxian froze solid, going stiff as an iron plank; helpless, he let himself be dragged by the collar, shuffling forward one agonizing step at a time.

Jiang Cheng found an empty room and hurled Wei Wuxian straight inside. The door banged shut behind them, and the spiritual hound trotted in, planting itself right by the threshold. Wei Wuxian kept his eyes glued to the beast, braced for it to tear into him at any given second. Replaying the past few moments—and how thoroughly he'd been neutralized—he couldn't help a dry thought:Jiang Cheng truly knows my every weakness.

Unrushed, Jiang Cheng settled down by the table and poured himself a cup of tea.

A thick, suffocating silence fell between them. Steam curled from the cup, but before taking a single sip, Jiang Cheng violently slammed it against the floor, shattering porcelain and splashing scalding tea across the boards.

The corner of Jiang Cheng’s mouth curled into a bitter, dangerous line. "Don't you have anything to say to me?"

Growing up together, Jiang Cheng had watched Wei Wuxian scramble up trees to escape barking dogs more times than he could count. He could bluster and play the fool around strangers, but in front of the one person who knew him down to his bones, all excuses fell apart. This was an interrogation far harder to survive than any lash from Zidian.

Wei Wuxian looked back at him, answering with flat honesty: "I don't know what you want me to say."

Jiang Cheng’s voice went dangerously soft. "Still unrepentant, I see."

Back in the day, their conversations had always been a rapid-fire trade of banter and barbed insults. Without skipping a beat, Wei Wuxian fired back, "And you haven't grown an inch, either."

Jiang Cheng let out a furious, humorless bark of laughter. "Fine. Let's see which one of us hasn't grown."

Without shifting from his chair, he barked a short command. The hound snapped to its feet!

Just breathing the same air as the beast had already broken Wei Wuxian into a cold sweat. Seeing that massive hound—half as tall as a man, baring jagged fangs, ears pinned back with razor-sharp intent—bearing down on him with a low, gutter rattle in its throat, a violent numbness shot from the soles of his feet straight to his skull. He’d long forgotten most of his childhood wanderings, but the sheer terror of being chased through frozen alleys, of teeth and claws tearing into raw flesh, remained etched into his marrow. It was a primal fear impossible to outgrow or rationalize away.

Suddenly, Jiang Cheng glanced sideways, eyes narrowing. "Who were you calling for?"

Wei Wuxian’s soul had practically evacuated his body; he couldn't even remember if he’d yelled a name. Only when Jiang Cheng barked the hound down did his scattered wits finally snap back. Staring blankly for a second, he jerked his head away.

Jiang Cheng pushed himself up from the table. A riding crop hung loosely from his hip, and resting his palm against it, he leaned down to study Wei Wuxian’s face. After a lingering pause, he straightened up, drawling, "Come to think of it, I forgot to ask: since when have you and Lan Wangji been this close?"

The realization hit Wei Wuxian instantly—he knew exactly whose name had slipped past his lips.

Jiang Cheng’s smile turned razor-sharp. "Back on Dafan Mountain, he went out of his way to shield you. Really makes a man wonder why."

A beat later, he corrected himself with a sneer: "No, that's not quite right. Lan Wangji wasn't necessarily shieldingyou. After all, the Gusu Lan Clan hasn't forgotten the havoc you and your loyal lapdog wreaked. A paragon of virtue, put on a pedestal by the entire world—how could a man like that ever stomach you? More likely, he has some history with this stolen body of yours."

Every syllable dripped with venomous mockery, wrapping insults inside thinly veiled compliments. Wei Wuxian couldn't take it anymore. "Watch your mouth."

Jiang Cheng countered, "I’ve never watched my tongue. Did you forget that, too?"

"Fair point," Wei Wuxian muttered dryly.

Jiang Cheng scoffed. "You have the nerve to tell me to watch my mouth? Did you watch yours when you spoke to Jin Ling on Dafan Mountain?"

Wei Wuxian’s expression froze.

Scoring a direct hit, Jiang Cheng’s mood visibly brightened, his voice slick with cruel amusement. "'Got a mother to birth you, but no mother to raise you'—what a line. Truly inspired. You’re the reason people talk behind his back today! You have such a convenient memory, don't you? Forgetting your words, forgetting your oaths... But tell me, do you remember how his parents died?!"

Wei Wuxian snapped his head up. "I haven't forgotten! I just..."

The words caught in his throat. He couldn't find an ending to that sentence.

"Just what? Lost for words?" Jiang Cheng sneered. "Doesn't matter. You can crawl back to Lotus Pier, kneel before my parents' memorial tablets, and take all the time you need to explain."

Wei Wuxian forced himself to keep his breathing level, his mind racing for an escape. He dreamed of returning to Lotus Pier every single day, but never to the unrecognizable, hollow shell it had become.

Heavy footsteps came pounding up the corridor, followed by frantic banging against the wood. Jin Ling's voice shouted from the hall: "Uncle!"

Jiang Cheng barked toward the door, "I told you to stay put! What do you want now?!"

"Uncle, I have something urgent to tell you!"

"If it was that important, why didn't you open your mouth when I was tearing into you earlier? Why bring it up now?!"

Jin Ling snapped right back, "Because you were yelling at me, that's why! Do you want to hear it or not?! If you don't care, I won't bother!"

Fuming, Jiang Cheng yanked the door open. "Spit it out and get lost!"

The boy stepped inside, freshly changed into crisp white robes. "I really did run into trouble today," he said quickly. "I think I saw Wen Ning!"

Jiang Cheng’s brow twitched violently. His hand dropped onto his sword hilt, his voice dripping murder: "When? Where?!"

"This afternoon," Jin Ling rattled off. "A few dozenlisouth, there's an abandoned shack. I heard rumors of an anomaly and checked it out, but there was a fierce corpse holed up inside."

Jin Ling delivered the lie with complete conviction, but to Wei Wuxian, it sounded like pure, unadulterated nonsense. He knew exactly where Jin Ling had been this afternoon. Besides, once Wen Ning went to ground, an inexperienced junior had zero chance of stumbling onto him unless Wei Wuxian summoned him out.

"Why the hell didn't you mention this earlier?!" Jiang Cheng demanded.

"I wasn't sure!" Jin Ling shot back defensively. "The corpse moved like lightning; the second I stepped through the door, it bolted. I only caught a glimpse of its back, but I heard the iron chains rattling—just like on Dafan Mountain. That's why I figured it might be him. If you hadn't chewed me out the second I walked in, I would've told you immediately. If he gets away because you wasted time yelling, that's on your rotten temper, not me!"

The boy tried to crane his neck to peek inside, but Jiang Cheng slammed the door in his face. "I'll settle this with you later! Scram!"

A muffled "Fine" echoed from the hall, followed by retreating footsteps.

As Jiang Cheng turned back around, Wei Wuxian quickly assembled a theatrical cocktail of pure panic, caught-red-handed dread, and helpless despair. The kid was sharper than he looked—he knew Jiang Cheng hated Wen Ning above all else and had crafted the perfect, seamless bait. Jiang Cheng already knew the Yiling Laozu and the Ghost General were practically glued at the hip, so hearing the corpse was nearby made him sixty percent a believer; seeing Wei Wuxian’s panicked expression bumped that up to eighty. More importantly, the sheer mention of Wen Ning made Jiang Cheng's blood boil so hot that all common sense evaporated.

Suffocating on bottled rage, Jiang Cheng cracked his whip against the floorboards right beside Wei Wuxian’s boots. "You really drag that obedient dog of yours everywhere you go!"

Wei Wuxian looked up at him. "He's already dead, and I've died once myself. What more do you want?"

Jiang Cheng leveled the crackling lash straight at his face. "What do I want?! Slaying him ten thousand times over wouldn't quench my hatred! He slipped through the cracks back then, but that ends today. I'm going to track him down, burn him to ash, and scatter his remains right in front of your face!"

Slamming the door behind him, he marched into the parlor, barking orders at Jin Ling: "Keep your eyes pinned on that man inside! Don't believe a word he says, and don't listen to him! If he makes a sound, or if he even thinks about whistling or playing a flute, gag him! If that doesn't work, chop his hands off and cut out his tongue!"

Wei Wuxian knew those threats were shouted loud enough for his benefit, a blunt warning to stay in line. Leaving him behind was simply a precaution so he couldn't take the reins and turn Wen Ning against them during the hunt.

Jin Ling answered with casual indifference: "Got it. As if I can't even watch one person. Uncle, why did you lock yourself in there with that cutsleeve anyway? What did he do this time?"

"None of your business," Jiang Cheng snapped. "Just guard the door. If he's gone when I get back, I'll break your legs!"

Extracting a few more details about the location, Jiang Cheng mobilized half his retinue and set off to hunt down a ghost that didn't exist.

After a few tense minutes, Jin Ling’s arrogant voice rang out from the corridor: "You, watch that corner. You, take the side entrance. The rest of you, hold the main gate. I'm going inside to deal with him."

Not daring to question the young master, the Jiang disciples saluted and dispersed. Seconds later, the door creaked open, and Jin Ling poked his head in, eyes darting about.

Wei Wuxian sat up. Jin Ling pressed a single finger against his lips, slipped quietly into the room, and laid his hand over Zidian, murmuring an incantation.

A weapon of Zidian’s caliber recognized only its master, but Jiang Cheng had clearly granted Jin Ling spiritual clearance. The purple electricity retracted in an instant, shrinking down into a sleek silver ring set with a glittering amethyst, dropping smoothly into the boy's palm.

Jin Ling whispered, "Move."

Having scattered the Jiang guards with nonsensical patrol routes, the two slipped through the window and cleared the compound walls without a sound. Leaving the inn behind, they sprinted through the dark streets until they ducked into a quiet grove of trees.

Hearing a rustle behind them, Wei Wuxian glanced back—and nearly had a heart attack. "Why the hell is that thing following us?! Tell it to get lost!"

Jin Ling blew two short whistles. The hound panted with its tongue out, letting out a soft, obedient whine, its perked ears dropping as it turned and trotted away.

Jin Ling crossed his arms, scoffing in disgust. "Look at you, pathetic. Fairy never bites people; he just looks intimidating. He's a trained spiritual beast that only attacks monsters and evil spirits. You think he's some common stray?"

Wei Wuxian held up a hand. "Wait. What did you just call him?"

"Fairy. That's his name."

Wei Wuxian stared. "You named a houndFairy?!"

Jin Ling stood his ground. "What's wrong with that? When he was a puppy, I called him Little Fairy. He grew up, so naturally, I dropped the 'Little'!"

Wei Wuxian shook his head in absolute horror. "No, no, no, the problem isn't the size! Who taught you how to name pets?!"

Like uncle, like nephew.Back in the day, Jiang Cheng had kept a few puppies at Lotus Pier, saddling them with names like Jasmine, Princess, and Sweetie—sounding more like courtesans than guard dogs.

"Real men don't sweat the small stuff," Jin Ling snapped, blushing. "Why are you obsessing over a name?! Stop! You crossed my uncle; if you stay in his hands, you'll be lucky to leave with half your life. I let you out, so we're even."

Wei Wuxian studied him. "Do you know why he locked me up?"

"Obviously. He thinks you're Wei Wuxian."

He doesn't just think it,Wei Wuxian mused.He caught the right man.

He pressed, "And what about you? Don't you suspect me?"

"My uncle does this all the time," Jin Ling said with a shrug. "He'd rather grab ten innocent people than let a single soul-snatcher walk. But since Zidian didn't rip your soul out, I'm willing to give you the benefit of the doubt. Besides, Wei Wuxian wasn't a cutsleeve, while you... you actually dared to go after..."

He trailed off, shivering in visceral disgust, before aggressively waving his hands as if shooing away a plague. "Anyway, your business with the Lanling Jin Clan is finished! If you want to throw tantrums, do it somewhere else—stay away from my family, or I won't let you off easy!"

Turning on his heel, Jin Ling took several strides before glancing over his shoulder. "What are you still standing there for? Waiting for my uncle to come drag you back? Let me tell you: don't think I owe you anything just because you pulled me out of that wall, and don't you dare expect any sappy gratitude from me!"

Wei Wuxian clasped his hands behind his back and ambled forward. "Kid, in this life, there are two sappy phrases you simply have to learn to say."

Jin Ling frowned. "Which two?"

"'Thank you,' and 'I'm sorry.'"

Jin Ling sneered, "I won't say either, and nobody can make me."

"One of these days, you'll be crying them through tears."

Jin Ling spat on the ground.

Wei Wuxian’s tone shifted, quiet and completely sincere: "I'm sorry."

Jin Ling blinked, caught off guard. "What?"

"Back on Dafan Mountain," Wei Wuxian said softly. "What I said to you... I'm sorry."

Jin Ling had been called 'a child with a mother to birth him, but no mother to raise him' more times than he could count, but he had never received an earnest, solemn apology for it. The sudden words hit him like a splash of cold water, leaving him entirely at a loss, fidgeting with awkward discomfort.

He waved his arms frantically, huffing, "Whatever! You're not the first person to throw that in my face. It's true—I don't have a mother to raise me. But that doesn't make me worse than anyone else! One of these days, I'll make every last one of you look at me and see that I'm ten times better than the lot of you!"

Wei Wuxian’s lips curved into a gentle smile. Just as he opened his mouth, his face dropped into theatrical horror. "Jiang Cheng?! You!"

Guilty over stealing Zidian and breaking a prisoner out, Jin Ling whipped around in pure panic. Seizing the opening, Wei Wuxian brought the edge of his palm chopping down against the boy's neck.

Catching Jin Ling before he hit the ground, Wei Wuxian laid him flat on the grass and hitched his trouser leg up to inspect the Malignant Curse Mark. He tried several dispelling techniques, but the black rot refused to recede. Knowing how lethal it was, he let out a low, heavy sigh.

He couldn't cleanse it, but he could do the next best thing: transfer the curse onto himself.

Jin Ling stirred awake a short while later, rubbing his aching neck. His temper flared the second he realized what had happened, leaping to his feet and ripping his sword free. "You hit me! Even my uncle has never laid a hand on me!"

Wei Wuxian blinked in exaggerated shock. "Really? Doesn't he constantly threaten to break your legs?"

"He's just venting!" Jin Ling yelled, face flushed. "You filthy cutsleeve, what the hell are you playing at?! I—"

Wei Wuxian ducked behind his own hands, yelling toward the empty woods: "Ah! Hanguang-jun!"

Jin Ling feared Lan Wangji even more than he feared his own uncle. After all, Jiang Cheng was family, while Hanguang-jun was an untouchable, terrifying outsider. Panicking, the boy wheeled around and sprinted for the road, screaming over his shoulder as he ran: "You lunatic! You dead cutsleeve! I'm remembering this! We're not finished!"

Wei Wuxian doubled over, laughing so hard he could barely draw breath. Once the boy's footsteps dissolved into the night, a dull tightness settled in his chest, breaking the laughter into a quiet fit of coughing.

Sitting back against a tree, his mind drifted backward.

He had been nine years old when Jiang Fengmian carried him home.

His own memories of that time were a blur, but Jin Ling's mother, Jiang Yanli, had remembered every detail, recounting them to him over the years.

She told him that after her father caught wind that Wei Wuxian’s parents had fallen in battle, he spent years scouring the land for their orphaned son. He finally tracked the boy down in Yiling. The first time Jiang Fengmian saw him, the child was kneeling in the dirt, scrounging for discarded fruit rinds in the gutter.

Winters and springs in Yiling were bitterly cold. The boy had been dressed in paper-thin, threadbare rags, the knees worn straight through, wearing mismatched shoes that didn't fit his feet. When Jiang Fengmian called out to him, the child remembered only that his name had a 'Ying' in it, and looked up. His cheeks were cracked and raw from the frost, yet his face was split into a bright, easy grin.

Jiang Yanli had told him that he was simply born with a smiling face. No matter how deep the grief, he never let it weigh him down; no matter how dire the circumstances, he could always find a reason to smile. It sounded a bit heartless to some, but to her, it was a blessing.

Jiang Fengmian had fed him a slice of melon, and the child had let the man scoop him up and carry him home. Back then, Jiang Cheng had been eight or nine himself, keeping a litter of puppies at Lotus Pier to play with. Discovering Wei Wuxian was terrified of dogs, Jiang Fengmian had gently asked his son to send the pups away. Jiang Cheng had thrown an absolute fit—smashing furniture, crying, and storming about—before finally conceding and giving the dogs away.

Though Jiang Cheng had harbored a bitter grudge over it for quite some time, once they grew close, they became an inseparable pair of terrors, raising hell across Yunmeng. Whenever they ran into stray dogs, it was always Jiang Cheng who chased them off with a stick, before spending the next ten minutes relentlessly mocking Wei Wuxian while the boy cowered at the top of a tree.

He had always assumed that when the dust settled, Jiang Cheng would stand by his side, while Lan Wangji would remain on the opposite bank.

He never could have guessed that reality would flip completely on its head.

Wei Wuxian walked slowly toward the agreed rendezvous spot. The street lanterns had burned low, and not a single soul wandered the quiet road. He didn't need to search; that pristine white silhouette was standing right at the end of the thoroughfare, head tilted slightly downward, unmoving.

Before Wei Wuxian could call out, Lan Wangji raised his head and locked eyes with him.

After a beat of dead silence, Lan Wangji began walking toward him, his expression darker than midnight.

Without meaning to, Wei Wuxian took a half-step back.

He could've sworn he saw faint, crimson threads of broken blood vessels swimming behind those pale eyes.

Truth be told... that look on Lan Wangji's face was genuinely terrifying.
